Drag the technologies into the right box – or tap a card, then the box.
Drag the slider: the cross-section of the pile next to a person, to scale – and which technologies come into question.
Choose a method: the animation shows how the machine works, and the card in what soil and with how much noise and vibration.
Set the hammer and the soil, then strike – one blow at a time or continuously. Watch the set and the driving record: where does the pile stop, and why?
Tune the vibrator! Find the frequency at which the soil resistance is smallest – and see what jetting adds, and what cohesive soil cannot do.

Choose a technology and a neighbouring building, and move the piling location. The curves are order-of-magnitude values from a simplified attenuation model; the faint curves show the other technologies.
Plan view at a given depth as the pile diameter “opens up”. On the left the soil is drilled out, on the right it is pushed aside – the graph below shows the grain density around the pile.
Step through or play the construction. The size of the bulb is given by the number of rammed concrete batches – watch how many times the base area grows.
Choose a drilling head, diameter, length and soil, and start drilling: the monitor shows the depth, the torque and the concrete pressure – and below, how much soil did NOT come up.
Choose a tool and watch its working cycle in the bore. Which soil is it for?
Set the soil, the groundwater, the depth and the method of support. Does the bore stand – or collapse?
A slurry-filled bore with the reinforcement cage in it. Keep the end of the pipe in the concrete – and see what happens if it comes out.
You are the rig operator: pull up the auger and feed the concrete. The record shows everything.
Enter the site and the pile – we show which bored technology comes into question, and why. (An indicative, illustrative assessment.)
The wall of an old apartment block stands on an overloaded, cracked strip footing. Step through how the micropiles take over the load – from the cellar, without demolishing the house.
The slender pile is “bedded” laterally by the soil – the softer the soil, the less. Set the soil strength and the free length, and watch when buckling governs instead of yielding of the steel.
Choose a soil and a jet variant, set the pressure, the lifting speed and the rotation speed – then build an overlapping wall from it. What happens if the returning spoil cannot escape?
Four kinds of element are made in the same soft soil. See how the tool works and what remains in the soil afterwards.
